title: How Lonely Lies the City
summary: Jerusalem, once full of people, sits like a widow with no one to comfort her. A narrator describes her humiliation, exile, and ruin, and admits that she has sinned greatly. Then the city speaks for herself, asking every passer-by whether any sorrow is like hers, confessing her rebellion, and pleading with the LORD to see her pain and to deal with her enemies as he has dealt with her.
story: The book of Lamentations opens just after the worst has happened. Jerusalem has fallen to Babylon, the temple has been burned, the king has been captured, and many of the people have been taken away. The prophets, above all Jeremiah, had warned that this would come if the people kept breaking their covenant with God, and it has. This first poem does not describe the siege itself so much as its aftermath: the empty streets, the silent festivals, the gloating enemies. It sets the tone for the whole book by letting grief speak without being hurried toward explanation, and by giving the ruined city a voice of her own.
historical:
The poem looks back on the fall of Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. After a siege of about a year and a half, famine inside the walls, and a breach in the summer, the Babylonian commander Nebuzaradan burned the temple, the royal palace, and the houses of the city and led many survivors into exile (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 52). A poorer remnant was left to work the land under a governor appointed by Babylon.

Several details reflect that history. Judah has gone into exile (verse 3). No pilgrims come to the appointed feasts (verse 4), because the temple is gone. Foreigners have entered the sanctuary (verse 10), which the law had closed to them. The city's lovers and friends (verses 2 and 19) are probably the allies Judah had trusted, such as Egypt and the small neighboring kingdoms that had joined in plotting revolt against Babylon (Jeremiah 27:3). None came to help, and some turned against her. The people trade their treasures for food (verse 11), a detail that fits the famine of the siege and the scarcity that followed.
cultural:
The poem pictures Jerusalem as a woman, a common way of speaking of cities in the ancient Near East and throughout the prophets, who call Jerusalem the Daughter of Zion. Here she is a widow (verse 1), which in ancient Israel meant more than grief: a widow often lost her protection, her income, and her standing, and the law repeatedly commands care for her because she was so vulnerable. She was a princess and is now a forced laborer. The image of her nakedness and stained skirts (verses 8 and 9) draws on the language of public shame and ritual uncleanness, since in Israel's purity laws certain bodily conditions made a person unclean and set them apart from worship. The city that was meant to be holy is now treated as untouchable.

Funerals in Israel included public laments, often led by professional mourning women, which followed a recognizable form: they began with a cry of how (in Hebrew ekah), contrasted what was with what is, and called on others to weep. Lamentations takes up that funeral song and applies it to a whole city. The repeated complaint that there is no one to comfort her reflects the custom of friends and relatives coming to sit with the bereaved. Jerusalem has no one.
literary: The chapter is an acrostic: its twenty-two stanzas begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, each stanza three lines long. The form gives order to chaos and suggests that grief is being expressed fully, from beginning to end. Most lines use the falling rhythm of the lament (a longer half-line followed by a shorter one). The poem has two main voices. A narrator speaks about Jerusalem in verses 1 to 11, but Zion breaks in with cries of her own (verses 9 and 11). From verse 12 to the end, Zion speaks directly, with one brief interruption from the narrator (verse 17). The refrain that there is no one to comfort her, or me, appears five times (verses 2, 9, 16, 17, and 21), binding the poem together and building to the plea that the LORD himself would look.

outline.t: The narrator: the widowed city and her lost splendor
The narrator: Jerusalem's sin and shame, and her cries to the LORD
Zion speaks: Is any sorrow like mine
The narrator: no one to comfort her
Zion confesses and prays for justice

doctrines.note: The chapter lets suffering be described in full before any lesson is drawn. God's people are allowed, even invited, to speak their grief aloud. The repeated cry that there is no one to comfort shows that loneliness is part of suffering, and that the Bible takes it seriously.

The poem does not deny the cause: “Jerusalem has sinned greatly” (verse 8), and Zion herself says, “The LORD is righteous, for I have rebelled against His command” (verse 18). Confession and grief are held together; admitting guilt does not make the pain less real.
Zion turns her pain into petition: “Look, O LORD, on my affliction” and “See, O LORD, how distressed I am” (verses 9 and 20). Prayer here is not polished; it is a cry for God to see.

words.note: Ekah, how. The first word of the book and its Hebrew title. It was the traditional opening cry of a funeral lament, an exclamation of shock at the distance between what was and what is. It returns at the start of chapters 2 and 4.

Nacham, to comfort, and in other forms to be sorry or to relent. The poem's refrain is that there is no one to comfort her (menachem, the comforter). The same verb opens Isaiah 40, “Comfort, comfort My people,” which many readers hear as God's answer to this chapter's cry.

Almanah, widow. In ancient Israel the widow was the model of the vulnerable person, without a husband's protection or provision, and God calls himself her defender (Psalm 68:5). Calling Jerusalem a widow says she has lost everyone who protected her.

Pesha, transgression or rebellion, a deliberate breach of a relationship or covenant, not a mere mistake. The poem uses it three times (verses 5, 14, and 22). Zion's transgressions are bound into a yoke on her neck: her sin has become her burden.

christ: Christian worship has long read this chapter during Holy Week, especially in the old Tenebrae services, and has heard verse 12 on the lips of Christ: “Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look around and see! Is there any sorrow like mine?” That use is an application, not a claim that the poet was predicting the cross; the speaker in the poem is the city. But the connection is not arbitrary. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), and on the cross he was mocked by those who passed by (Mark 15:29), abandoned by his friends, and made to bear sin not his own. Where Zion had no comforter, the New Testament presents Christ as the one who enters the place of the uncomforted, and the Spirit he sends is called the Comforter or Helper (John 14:16).

hard.q: If Jerusalem admits her sin, why does she still ask God to punish her enemies?
hard.a: Zion confesses that the LORD is righteous (verse 18) and then asks him to deal with her enemies as he has dealt with her (verses 21 and 22). Some readers find this vindictive. Others see a sense of justice: the nations that destroyed Jerusalem were not innocent tools but acted with cruelty and glee, and if God judges his own people for sin, he must also judge theirs. The prayer asks for equal justice, and it hands that justice to God rather than seeking revenge. It is also the prayer of a person in extreme pain, and the Bible records such prayers honestly without endorsing every feeling in them. The New Testament adds Jesus' command to love enemies, and it also affirms that God will judge justly (Romans 12:19). If you are reading this from your own place of loss and find that the anger or despair is too heavy to carry, don't carry it alone: talk to someone you trust, a pastor, a counselor, or a doctor, and if you are thinking of harming yourself, contact a crisis line now (in the United States, call or text 988).

questions: Jerusalem cries that there is no one to comfort her. Who in your life, or in your community, is grieving without anyone sitting beside them?
The poem holds confession and grief together. Why is it hard to admit fault and still feel free to mourn what was lost?
What would it look like for you to bring your own grief to God as honestly as Zion does here?
